<reason>PRO built a clean, durable path: opt-in cost borne by the chooser, matched rides remove exposure to the risk pool that produces nearly all driver-on-rider assaults, unmatched rides face only baseline risk, and displacement touches a small fraction of matches. CON's strongest framing—"enough" means working at the 11 p.m. suburban hour of fear—was well-articulated and its point that large rider pool onto thin driver pool differs from accessibility niches was fair. But PRO reframed decisively: incidents cluster where matching is thick too, and CON's standard would disqualify every partial safety measure. CON's attempt to name harms (walking after "no match," cream-skimming, recruited drivers seating men) was speculative and PRO's closing dismantled each as the status quo redescribed. CON never convincingly quantified the operational cost beyond asserting "identity ops," while PRO conceded the inefficiency honestly and sized it. PRO's two clipped turns are a minor execution cost but lost only trailing sentences.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's "name one rider whose risk goes up" pressure question followed by the arithmetic answer in [B4.1]-[B4.2], then the closing's takedown of CON's [A4.1] harms ("nearly-all to nearly-all," "exposure only by working hours she wasn't working") neutralized CON's central "rearranging who waits" claim.</best_rebuttal>
